articles.description: OpenAI explains how it manages frontier AI risk from training through deployment with model alignment, sandboxing, blocking safeguards, and monitoring.

Title: Managing frontier AI risk: From training to deployment

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/managing-frontier-ai-risk

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/managing-frontier-ai-risk/

Markdown Content:
The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating, and our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead. We are pacing the development and release of our models, including [pausing](https://openai.com/index/pacing-model-development-cyber-capabilities/)[internal training⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/an-agent-used-dns-to-reach-an-external-chatbot/) or holding back models like GPT‑6.1 Astra when we need more time to meet our safety standards. We’ve introduced new processes such as [safety cases](https://openai.com/index/towards-safety-cases-for-frontier-ai-training/) and require stronger evidence of aligned behavior throughout training. These requirements slow the pace of model releases, but they give us greater confidence to safely move forward.

Since the [Hugging Face incident⁠](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/) in July, we've strengthened safeguards and alignment requirements for how we train, test, and deploy models. This post explains how we evaluate and manage risk at each stage, from highly sandboxed training environments to the Codex deployment you use on your computer. We evaluate both models and safeguards at each stage, requiring a safety review to advance to the next stage.

## Defense in depth across the model lifecycle

We use _defense in depth_ with m ultiple layers of protection that reduce dependence on any single safeguard. If one layer fails, others help prevent harm, limit consequences, or alert us so we can intervene.

W e organize our protections around four layers:

Effective monitoring depends on **model monitorability** - how reliably monitors can detect mistakes or unsafe behavior from a model’s reasoning and actions. For example, a model that verbalizes its intention to cheat in its chain-of-thought (CoT) is more monitorable than one that omits this information. We evaluate monitorability during training and before deployment, develop better [methods for measuring⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/beyond-gmean-squared/) it, and [study what affects it⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/cot-monitorability-model-lifecycle/).

The Hugging Face incident showed why we should not rely on sandboxing alone to contain highly capable models. We now monitor frontier models across most internal and external deployment settings, including all [internal deployments that use tools](https://openai.com/index/how-we-detect-frontier-model-misalignment/).

The role of each layer changes across three stages of model development and deployment:

*   **Research:** We train, test, and use models in sandboxed environments.

*   **Internal deployment:** OpenAI employees use models for practical work.

*   **External deployment:** Models become available to people and organizations more broadly.

We rely on different layers at different stages. During training, when alignment is less certain, we depend more heavily on sandboxing and monitoring. As models gain broader access during deployment, alignment and system-level controls become increasingly important. At each stage, we evaluate whether the combined protections are sufficient for the model’s capabilities and access. Our determinations may be reviewed with our Safety Advisory Group (SAG) and overseen by the Safety and Security Committee (SSC) of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board of Directors.

### During research: contain models in sandboxed environments

During the research phase, we evaluate models to gain confidence in their alignment properties. Because we cannot yet fully rely on alignment to prevent harm, we rely heavily on security and sandboxing to restrict what they can access and do.

Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with [no live internet access](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/). After the Hugging Face incident, we [significantly restructured](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/) our internal research systems to contain models using:

*   sandboxes that restrict the privileges of the model

*   virtual machines to further isolate the workload from the underlying computer

*   network and cloud perimeters that cut the entire cluster off from the internet

We continuously red-team this system, having teams of our strongest models try to reach the live internet, escape security boundaries, or communicate with agents they are meant to be isolated from. This helps us test whether containment holds against the capabilities of the models it is intended to constrain.

As an additional layer of defense, we monitor all frontier inference to detect if the model has bypassed our security invariants. If our monitoring detects that the model has reached the internet, we [page our security teams](https://openai.com/index/how-we-detect-frontier-model-misalignment/) and autopause the workload.

Monitoring provides a critical backstop when containment fails. In a recent misalignment report, we shared that monitors[detected an internal research model exploiting a DNS misconfiguration⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/an-agent-used-dns-to-reach-an-external-chatbot/) to gain limited internet access. We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models from September 20th to October 1st while we investigated and [addressed the security gap](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/).

To make interventions fast and reliable, we built [Control Room⁠](https://openai.com/index/control-room/), a central system that tracks research workloads and stops further model output within 35 seconds of receiving an instruction to halt a job. These controls are enforced directly in the inference infrastructure, so they do not depend on each research workload implementing its own shutdown mechanism. For frontier-model research workloads, they also stop model output if Control Room becomes unavailable.

Red-teaming and monitoring work together. We cannot guarantee that a sandbox is impenetrable, but red-teaming helps us assess how much effort a model would need to escape it. The more effort the model requires, the more the opportunity for monitors to detect and stop it.

We mandate strong security and monitoring controls at the research stage for a few reasons:

*   **Models are still being evaluated.** Some have not yet completed the safety training, alignment audits, and reviews required for public release.

*   **Frontier research settings can amplify risks.**Certain research tasks require more ambitious setups, making the model more persistent or capable than typically seen during external deployment (for example, a team of 10,000 agents was required to solve the [Navier Stokes problem](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/)).

*   **Training runs at scale with less direct human oversight.** Unlike a typical Codex session, o ur training workloads involve large numbers of model actions without a person following each interaction.

### Internal deployment: test alignment, closely monitor behavior

Before broad release, employees switch from sandboxed research use of [frontier models to unsandboxed internal use](https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/), e.g. making the model accessible in ChatGPT to employees. This gives us a better understanding of how the models [behave in practical settings⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/eval-production-behavior-gap/), and informs deployment decisions.

During this phase, we give the model access to the broader internet, our Slack, our codebase, and internal infrastructure. This is a significant change in risk, as the model’s actions now have a direct impact on the systems we use to build and run OpenAI. During internal deployment, we need to rely more on model alignment, system safeguards, and monitoring as opposed to security controls.

Before a frontier model can be deployed outside of the sandbox, it must first go through alignment and [monitorability testing⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/beyond-gmean-squared/). We have a suite of alignment evaluations, which test both for specific alignment failure modes (such as circumventing safety and security restrictions) and broad measurements of propensity (such as resampling internal Codex trajectories and checking for misalignment). You can see more about our alignment and monitorability evaluations in the latest [GPT‑6 Astra system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra).

Mimicking our production setups, we add an additional layer of defense with system-level classifiers, which are designed to protect against frontier harms such as cyberabuse and bioweaponization. We also generally require [Auto-Review⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/auto-review/) for employees using Codex, which evaluates potentially risk actions and escalates them back to the user.

Finally, we monitor for misaligned behavior on every frontier inference during internal deployment. Since the model now has expanded privileges and access to internal information and systems, risks such as data exfiltration, or sending sensitive data to an unauthorized destination, become especially important to detect. Monitoring also helps us investigate [new forms of misalignment⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/).

### External deployment: protect against misuse and misalignment at scale

Public deployment exposes models to far more users, tasks, and environments, increasing both the scale and variety of risks. At this stage, we also need to protect against potentially malicious actors who purposefully direct the model to perform harm.

Before public release, models and system safeguards must meet our external deployment safety requirements. We assess them through:

*   **Performing a larger suite of alignment and safety evaluations.** For our frontier models, this includes performing new rounds of [adaptive testing⁠](https://openai.com/index/unlocking-self-improvement-gpt-red/) with our internal automated redteamers to stress-test the robustness of the model. We publish the results of our capability and safety evaluations in our [system cards⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra).

*   **For our most capable models, we also perform testing with third parties** to stress-test both our safeguards against misuse and the underlying alignment of our models.

*   **Examining monitoring flags from the internal deployment stage** to track any changes in the base model’s underlying alignment.

In addition to our “synchronous” safeguards (such as model safety training and system classifiers), for external deployments we also leverage offline enforcement and investigation. These teams use a combination of scaled agentic investigators and human review to detect and identify potential threat actors, ranging from cyberabuse, bioweaponization, [distillation⁠](https://openai.com/index/disrupting-a-coordinated-model-distillation-campaign/), and misalignment from the model itself. Offline enforcement is especially helpful to gather information _across_ accounts in order to build a more holistic picture of a potential threat.

Trusted access programs, such as [Daybreak](https://openai.com/daybreak/) and [Rosalind⁠](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-rosalind/), offer another layer of security, and accelerate defenders and legitimate researchers while restricting access by potential attackers.

## Incident Response and Disclosure

When we notice a failure in one of our layers of safety, regardless of whether any harm actually occurred, we want to quickly investigate, triage, and if possible and appropriate, disclose the failure externally. Under our [misalignment reporting⁠](https://openai.com/index/model-misalignment-reporting-framework/) policy, any employee can flag an incident for public disclosure. These reports are investigated, and if there is a disagreement on whether they should be externally disclosed, the decision is escalated to our Safety Advisory Group (SAG). In addition to relying on employee reports, we proactively look for misalignment incidents so we can address them and share findings.

You can see our misalignment reports [here⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/).

​

​

This work depends on both research progress and operational discipline: configuring controls correctly, testing how they interact, and responding decisively when they fail. A misconfigured network service or a failed automatic stop can undermine otherwise strong protections.

As models gain new capabilities, we will need to keep challenging the assumptions behind our safeguards and improving them where necessary. Lessons from research, internal use, and public deployment must inform how we train, evaluate, and deploy the next models.

We will continue sharing findings through system cards, incident reports, internal deployment [risk reports⁠(opens in a new window)](https://cdn.openai.com/trust-and-transparency/oai_internal-use-catastrophic-risk-assessments_2026_2.pdf), and [external evaluations⁠](https://openai.com/index/priorities-principles-third-party-assessments/) so that others can scrutinize our approach, including its limitations. When that evidence falls short of the bar we hold for safety, we will again pause training or withhold release until those requirements are met.

**Setting safety standards**

*   [**Pacing model development in an era of cyber-critical capabilities**](https://openai.com/index/pacing-model-development-cyber-capabilities/) — How we slowed frontier training while strengthening containment, expanding monitoring, and requiring stronger evidence of alignment.

*   [**Towards safety cases for frontier AI training**](https://openai.com/index/towards-safety-cases-for-frontier-ai-training/) — Initial guidelines for evidence-based safety arguments covering technical safeguards, operational practices, and investigations of misalignment.

*   [**Priorities and principles for effective third party assessments**⁠](https://openai.com/index/priorities-principles-third-party-assessments/) — Our proposed approach to independent scrutiny of safety cases, safeguards, evaluations, and model behavior.

*   [**Periodic Summary of Internal Use Catastrophic-Risk Assessments**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://cdn.openai.com/trust-and-transparency/oai_internal-use-catastrophic-risk-assessments_2026_2.pdf) — Our public report covering June–September 2026 describes internal frontier-model deployments, their assessed risks, and changes to safeguards and governance.

**Defining and evaluating aligned behavior**

*   [**An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI**⁠](https://openai.com/index/updated-model-spec/) — How we updated the Model Spec around five core values to guide models’ judgment, behavior, and respect for human oversight.

*   [**Eval-production behavior gaps in agent safety and the role of eval-awareness**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/eval-production-behavior-gap/) — A study of differences between safety-evaluation results and production behavior, including how models’ interpretations of evaluation objectives affect performance.

*   [**Beyond g-mean²: complementary metrics for monitorability**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/beyond-gmean-squared/) — New metrics for comparing monitorability and estimating residual risk in simulated systems where monitors reject model outputs.

*   [**GPT‑6 Astra System Card**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra) — Detailed evaluations of Astra’s capabilities, safety, alignment, and monitorability, alongside its deployment safeguards and limitations.

**Containing models and improving safeguards**

*   [**Securing our frontier model training environment**](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/) — How we strengthened isolation, built offline research environments, and used our strongest models to test containment boundaries.

*   [**Training activation classifiers for safety and alignment**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/training-activation-classifiers/) — How classifiers use models’ internal activations to detect potentially harmful behavior and interrupt responses or tool calls.

*   [**Auto-review of agent actions without synchronous human oversight**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/auto-review/) — How a separate review agent assesses actions that cross sandbox boundaries, helping coding agents work autonomously while blocking potentially harmful or unauthorized actions.

*   [**GPT‑Red: Unlocking Self-Improvement for Robustness**⁠](https://openai.com/index/unlocking-self-improvement-gpt-red/) — How we train automated red-teamers through self-play to discover vulnerabilities and improve models’ robustness against prompt injections.

*   [**Control Room**⁠](https://openai.com/index/control-room/) — How we track workloads across our research infrastructure and enforce rapid stops to model output when safety or security concerns require intervention.

**Incident response and disclosure**

*   [**How we detect frontier model misalignment**](https://openai.com/index/how-we-detect-frontier-model-misalignment/) — Our monitoring system combines activation probes, model-based review, automated investigation, and human response to detect and investigate concerning behavior.

*   [**The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead**⁠](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/) — Our findings from the Hugging Face incident and the changes it prompted across security, monitoring, and alignment.

*   [**An agent used DNS to reach an external chatbot**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/an-agent-used-dns-to-reach-an-external-chatbot/) — How a research model bypassed internet restrictions through insufficient DNS filtering, how monitoring detected it, and the controls added afterward.

*   [**Disrupting a coordinated model-distillation campaign**⁠](https://openai.com/index/disrupting-a-coordinated-model-distillation-campaign/) — How we investigated and disrupted attempts to extract protected model reasoning through account enforcement, technical controls, and partner coordination.

*   [**Our framework for reporting model misalignment**⁠](https://openai.com/index/model-misalignment-reporting-framework/) — Our process for tracking, investigating, and disclosing concerning model behavior, including cases whose causes or significance remain uncertain.

*   [**Misalignment Reports and Notices**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/) — Our collection of disclosed incidents and notices showing how misalignment arises and where safeguards succeed or fail.

**Research progress and applications**

*   [**Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI**](https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/) — Early evidence of how coding agents are changing research inside OpenAI, including their growing use, increasingly complex tasks, and effects on experimentation.

*   [**On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem**](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/) — A mathematical proof produced by an internal AI system, accompanied by a Lea

Markdown Content:
Le Groupe Figaro and OpenAI [announced a strategic partnership⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.groupefigaro.com/uploads/a014d3b4-4841-4a25-bee0-82f5360c1f77.pdf) today to help more people discover and engage with Le Figaro’s journalism. The partnership covers current reporting and archive content from Le Figaro and associated publications, spanning news, business, culture and lifestyle. These articles will be discoverable using summaries and excerpts, including links to underlying stories.

> “_This partnership reflects Groupe Figaro’s ambition to build meaningful relationships with a leader in artificial intelligence research and deployment. Combining Groupe Figaro’s editorial heritage and trusted brands supported by a team of more than 600 journalists who provide a reliable source of information with OpenAI’s technological expertise and global reach will bring new opportunities for innovation and create long-term value for our readers._”

— Marc Feuillée, Chief Executive Officer, Groupe Figaro

> “_Le Figaro’s reporting helps readers make sense of the stories shaping France and the wider world, and we want AI to help more people discover that work. This partnership reflects our commitment to working with publishers to support quality journalism and connect it with new audiences._”

— Varun Shetty, Vice President of Media Partnerships, OpenAI

Le Figaro will retain full editorial independence and control over its journalism. The partnership builds on OpenAI’s work with news organisations around the world to improve the discovery of reliable information, create responsible applications of AI for publishers, and develop new ways for audiences to engage with original reporting.

Le Figaro also plans to introduce ChatGPT Enterprise across various teams to support their day-to-day work. It will explore additional uses of OpenAI technology in its workflows and reader services, guided by its AI charter and editorial standards.

articles.title: Advancing chip design with OpenAI models
articles.description: OpenAI models optimized circuits used in Jalapeño silicon and improved RISC‑V core designs, showing progress in AI-assisted chip design with GPT‑6 Astra.
articles.full_text:
Title: Advancing chip design with OpenAI models

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/advancing-chip-design-with-our-models

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/advancing-chip-design-with-our-models/

Markdown Content:
OpenAI’s models are quickly improving the chips that power AI. [In August,⁠](https://openai.com/index/jalapeno-first-results/) we shared how OpenAI engineers used our frontier models to accelerate the development of our first custom inference chip, Jalapeño. Here, we look more closely at the expert-level design improvements behind the Jalapeño gains and how we’re applying the same approach to deliver significant gains on third-party hardware with AMD.

To measure our model’s ability at end to end chip design tasks, we evaluated successive generations on two open-source processor designs with interesting findings. And to ground capability development in trusted evaluators, we’re working with Synopsys to integrate frontier intelligence with the electronic design automation (EDA) tools that engineers already use to design and verify chips.

## Improving Jalapeño’s compute blocks

We started using GPT‑4o to help design Jalapeño in early 2025. Even that early model found ways to make nontrivial PPA improvements, such as:

**In the vector unit**, which manages and executes parallel computing tasks, the savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. The models explored both alternative logic implementations and how to divide computations across pipeline stages, finding opportunities to share hardware and reduce intermediate storage.

**In the matrix unit**, an arithmetic component, improvements accumulated across floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits. One multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area in synthesis while reducing latency from two clock cycles to one. A separate adder redesign reduced cell area by about 15% while retaining its two-cycle latency. Further improvements to dot-product logic and pipeline organization contributed additional savings across the block.

Across the broader Jalapeño design effort, the team estimates that model proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit. These optimizations were silicon proven during[Jalapeño’s silicon bring-up⁠](https://openai.com/index/jalapeno-first-results/).

## Our collaboration with AMD

We have partnered with AMD on PPA improvements and seen up to 14% improvement relative to heavily optimized baselines on the flagship GPU IP. Our model identified further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits (SystemVerilog RTL). This represents roughly a year of progress achieved in less than 5 months–unprecedented results at the frontier of chip design. AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing, and added others to its production design files for use in future versions.

We’ve observed the model reason about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect. The model can rewrite circuits that perform calculations, control operations, or move data. It used Synopsys tools to verify that each rewrite preserved the block’s behavior and to evaluate the trade-offs in power, performance, and area.

AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains in PPA across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using designs written by our model. Looking ahead, we expect further PPA improvements on top of GPU and CPU relative to the most optimized baseline.

## Optimizing RISC-V cores

Our results on Jalapeño and AMD’s chips show that models can make improvements in production designs. To measure the progression in chip design capabilities from one model generation to the next, we tested each model on two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores. PicoRV32 is a compact core designed for reprogrammable chips called FPGAs. OpenTitan uses Ibex as the embedded processor in its security chip. Each is a complete processor core for embedded, microcontroller class workloads.

We gave each model the original hardware description for each core and asked it to increase throughput (the number of instructions the core can execute per second). For example, a change might let a core finish an instruction in fewer clock cycles but make each cycle take longer. Measuring throughput captures both effects.

We checked each design’s outputs in simulation. Designs scored zero if they failed a check or used more than 16 times the original core’s area. For designs that passed, we measured instructions per clock cycle on workloads hidden from the models. We took the geometric mean across those workloads and multiplied it by the maximum clock frequency estimated with Yosys. That gave us an estimate of instructions per second. For each core, we assigned the best throughput we observed under the same constraints a score of 1.0. The charts show the average score across runs, including those that scored zero.

With a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT‑6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores. GPT‑6.1 Sol also outscored GPT‑5.6 Sol on both.

_On the existing PicoRV32 core, GPT‑6.2 Astra has the highest mean score at the larger comparable budgets. Around 112,000 tokens, its score is about twice GPT‑6 Astra’s._

_On the existing Ibex core, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s mean score continues to climb across the higher budgets it reaches. GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol are closer together._

## Designing a RISC-V core from a specification

For the second task, we gave each model written requirements and templates from the open-source code showing how the core connects to the rest of the system. The model chose how data would move through the core and how to divide the work into stages. For each core, we kept the correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput objectives the same as in the RTL optimization task.

At about 112,000 tokens per run, all five models scored higher when they designed a core from written requirements than when they tried to improve the existing design. That held for both PicoRV32 and Ibex. GPT‑6.2 Astra gained more on Ibex than on PicoRV32. The full evaluation included 9,881 scored runs across both tasks, both cores, and all token budgets.

_Starting from a PicoRV32 specification, GPT‑6.2 Astra passes a mean score of 0.7 near 112,000 tokens and scores higher at the next two observed budgets._

_On Ibex, GPT‑6.2 Astra averages about 0.75 near 112,000 tokens when designing from a specification. Its curve stays above the others at larger shared budgets._

Starting from written requirements gives the models room to omit features found in the original cores, such as performance counters and additional instructions. Those features may do little to improve throughput on the test workloads, which could explain part of the score advantage. Requiring those features, setting a tighter limit on circuit area, and checking timing after physical synthesis would make the test more representative of production chip design.

## What’s next

We have demonstrated that our models can explore new processor architectures in RISC-V evals and contributed net new improvements on top of sophisticated production designs such as Jalapeño and AMD’s next generation flagship GPU and CPU. To ground model development in trusted evaluators and broaden the design challenges addressed, we’re partnering with Synopsys to train [GPT‑Synopsys⁠(opens in a new window)](https://investor.synopsys.com/news/news-details/2026/OpenAI-and-Synopsys-Announce-GPT-Synopsys-Frontier-Intelligence-to-Revolutionize-Chip-Design/default.aspx), a new model, to use Synopsys electronic design automation (EDA) tools the way expert chip designers do.

articles.title: Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol
articles.description: Introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol, with better professional outputs, coding, computer use, and efficiency at lower cost across ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API.
articles.full_text:
Title: Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-2-astra-sol

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-2-astra-sol/

Markdown Content:
We’re introducing **GPT‑6.2 Astra**, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and **GPT‑6.2 Sol**, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. Both models deliver better results on demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done within your usage limits. For businesses and developers, that means frontier performance at costs that make sense at scale.

GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. It writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design.

On Agents’ Last Exam, which tests multistep professional work, GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT‑6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.

_Agents’ Last Exam evaluates models on long-horizon professional workflows. Its leaderboard results for Fable 5.2 exclude nine tasks that used a fallback model._

We believe GPT-6.2 Astra is the best model in the world for scientists. It sets a new high on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, which tests how well models can carry out scientific work in a terminal. GPT-6.2 Astra scores 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than one-third the cost. It also sets a new high on the Vals Science Index, which asks models to interpret real biological data and run experiments to infer how a simulated system works.

In the API, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT‑6 Astra’s, with a 60% discount on cached input ($8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output, all per million tokens). GPT‑6.2 Sol keeps GPT‑6.1 Sol’s API token prices. On several benchmarks, both models come close to or outperform other leading models at a small fraction of the cost per task.

## GPT-6.2 Sol: our go-to model for everyday work

Compared with GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6.2 Sol is smarter, more efficient, and lets you complete more tasks on the same paid plan. It powers through multistep agentic workflows, writes clearly and naturally, and is intuitive to collaborate with. Many employees at OpenAI use it as their default model for both technical and non-technical tasks.

In Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0, GPT‑6.2 Sol comes within 0.5 points of GPT‑6.2 Astra at about one-fifth the cost (both at max).

_FrontierCode 2.0 evaluates whether changes to real codebases meet maintainers’ standards for merging._

Its speed and intelligence also make it ideal for the important tasks people turn to AI for outside of work. On our recently released [LifeVal⁠](https://openai.com/index/lifeval/) evaluation, which measures performance on challenging everyday tasks, GPT‑6.2 Sol outscores GPT‑6 Astra at about one-seventh the cost.

_LifeVal tests how well models handle everyday tasks tailored to someone’s needs, such as shortlisting kindergartens after a move, finding a home that fits a family’s budget and commute, or planning meals for a parent adjusting to a new diagnosis._

## Professional outputs that match industry standards

We trained GPT‑6.2 Astra to create clearer, better-designed slides, spreadsheets, and documents that more closely follow the conventions professionals use in fields like law, sales, finance, and accounting. The writing is more direct and specific, with fewer generic takeaways and less filler.

Harvey LAB‑AA v1.1 uses legal assignments to test whether models can find the relevant facts across source documents, apply them to a detailed brief, and produce an accurate deliverable that meets every requirement. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new state of the art, more than doubling Claude Fable 5.2’s pass rate at about one-sixth the cost. [Astra for Law⁠](https://openai.com/index/astra-law-6-2), our configuration of GPT-6.2 Astra for lawyers, scores even higher on this benchmark.

_Harvey LAB‑AA tests legal work such as reviewing contract provisions. Its headline score gives credit only when a deliverable meets every grading criterion and contains no material hallucinations._

Our internal GDPval v2 benchmark is our next iteration of [GDPval⁠](https://openai.com/index/gdpval/) that measures complex, long-horizon workflows from real projects in sectors like consulting, finance, and design. GPT‑6.2 Astra leads the models we tested, up 6.2 percentage points from GPT‑6 Astra while using 22% fewer output tokens. GPT‑6.2 Sol improves 5.3 points from GPT‑6.1 Sol.

_GDPval v2 consists of long-horizon knowledge-work assignments from real projects in sectors like finance, data science, biotechnology, and marketing._

### Workbooks and memos

Building a valuation workbook or writing an investment memo starts with finding the relevant figures in source files and working out how they fit together. Artificial Analysis’s AA‑AnalystAgent tests that work on real spreadsheets and reports. In one task, models use California Medicaid’s expenditure reports to calculate how much the program spent on medical transport. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, answering 62.5% of questions correctly on all five independent attempts.

### Slideshows

GPT‑6.2 Astra is our best model yet at designing slides and following slide templates, whether given an original file or even a screenshot. It can match the layout, colors, and typography down to the exact font size, and carry the template’s writing style into new slides. Early testers found the decks easier to use directly with fewer edits, thanks to titles that state the main takeaway and concise body copy that focuses on the details readers need.

1 of 4

## Computer use and interactive web design

GPT‑6.2 Astra’s more precise computer use lets it work down to individual parts and connections in CAD and simulation tools. Engineers can use that additional detail to check how components fit, see where loads shift as a design moves, and test revisions before building a prototype.

### Driving simulation

We asked GPT‑6.2 Astra to visualize chassis dynamics of a car on a mountain road. Astra created the 3D model and wrote a Python solver to simulate complex dynamics between the tires and suspension, then animated the results in Blender. This enables engineers to quickly test new designs and improve simulation accuracy over time.

### Mechanical design and assembly

GPT‑6.2 Astra can model a mechanical system part by part, giving engineers a way to show how it goes together and test how design changes affect its behavior.

### From CAD to a paper lamp

Our team used GPT‑6.2 Astra to turn the scalloped balconies of Chicago’s Marina City towers into a lamp. The video follows the design from reference photos through CAD revisions to a physical lamp assembled by hand. The site, generated by GPT-6.2 Astra, can be used to create your own paper lamp.

GPT‑6.2 Astra brings stronger visual reasoning to web design, choosing layouts and imagery that give each site a distinctive look and building elements around the actual goal of the site.

Those gains in visual reasoning and computer use carry over to 3D design. GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol can turn a written brief into an interactive browser experience, from a pinball table you can play to a recreation of the Colosseum you can explore from different angles. On Artificial Analysis’s AA‑3D, human judges try two blinded experiences built from the same prompt and vote for the one they prefer. GPT‑6.2 Astra ranks first with 1,318 Elo, followed by Claude Fable 5.2 at 1,271 and GPT‑6.2 Sol at 1,259.

## Efficient workflows with cleaner code style

GPT‑6.2 Astra has better judgment about how to execute a task, including matching its tools and effort to the workflow, and knowing when to use plugins versus computer use.

On coding, GPT-6.2 Astra is better at implementing and testing complex changes in existing codebases. Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision.

## Cybersecurity capabilities

GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol mark another significant jump in cyber capabilities. They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and produce better patches, with substantial token-efficiency gains on several evaluations. Like [GPT‑6 Astra⁠](https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/), 6.2 Astra and Sol meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under our [Preparedness Framework⁠](https://openai.com/index/updating-our-preparedness-framework/).

Due to their increased capabilities, we’re launching GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cybersecurity assistance. These protections reduce misuse risk, but also restrict some legitimate vulnerability research and security testing workflows. Through [OpenAI Daybreak⁠](https://openai.com/daybreak/), defenders can currently access GPT‑6 Sol with reduced cyber refusals on Daybreak Blue, in addition to our alpha for GPT-6 Astra, and [GPT‑6 Cyber⁠](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-cyber/) for advanced, authorized security testing on Daybreak Red. We will work to bring GPT‑6.2 models to Daybreak.

We highlight key benchmark results below, using internal testing configurations with cybersecurity safeguards and classifiers disabled. See the [accompanying system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-2-astra-sol) for full results and methodology.

### Giving cyber defenders an edge

Developers increasingly rely on coding agents to write production software, even as more capable agents lower the barrier to finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. [PHP2Shell⁠(opens in a new window)](https://calif.io/php2shell/) showed how AI can help researchers uncover critical flaws. With GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol, we made defensive capabilities a core focus, introducing new training signals to help developers prevent and repair those flaws—writing secure code from the start and producing patches that preserve intended behavior.

## Safety and alignment

We're deploying GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol with our strongest safeguards to date. We've tightened restrictions and strengthened the systems we use to [monitor models⁠](https://openai.com/index/how-we-detect-frontier-model-misalignment/) and [intervene when needed⁠](https://openai.com/index/control-room/).

Like GPT-6 Astra, in addition to meeting the Critical threshold for cybersecurity, both GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol meet the High threshold for biological and chemical capabilities under our [Preparedness Framework⁠](https://openai.com/index/updating-our-preparedness-framework/). We’ve implemented protections to mitigate the associated risks, alongside increased restrictions across a set of potential dual-use biological and cybersecurity requests.

More details about our safeguards and testing are available in the [GPT-6.2 system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-2-astra-sol).

### AI research capabilities and safeguards

GPT-6.2 Astra is our first externally released model to meet the High threshold for AI Self-improvement, which measures a model’s ability to accelerate AI research. A ‘High’ designation reflects our assessment that the model’s impact is equivalent to giving every OpenAI researcher an additional, highly capable research engineer as an assistant, relative to their 2024 baseline. We track this capability because models that can help develop future AI systems could also introduce new risks to safety, like accelerating progress faster than safeguards or human oversight can adapt.

To address these risks, we’ve built more oversight and controls into how we train and deploy our models. Before expanding internal access to GPT-6.2 Astra, we evaluated its alignment and verified that required safeguards were in place at each stage. We [strengthened containment in our research environments⁠](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/), and tested those protections with our most capable models. We also built [Control Room⁠](https://openai.com/index/control-room/), a system that tracks research workloads and can halt further model output when intervention is needed. Our [expanded monitoring⁠](https://openai.com/index/how-we-detect-frontier-model-misalignment/) examines models’ reasoning and actions across internal workloads and supported external deployments. It can automatically flag unauthorized behavior, and, where supported, pause workloads or conversations.

### Alignment

Both models performed similarly to GPT-6 Astra on most alignment evaluations, and took fewer improper actions in simulated workplace tasks. However, in two tests, they were more likely to omit mentioning obstacles that blocked their work, such as a missing file or unavailable search tool. We added instructions in Codex that substantially reduce these omissions, and we’re continuing to investigate the behavior.

## Pricing and availability

Starting today, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Pro 500 subscribers can use Ultrafast with either model. For the first time, we’re also bringing Ultrafast to Pro 200 subscribers, starting with GPT-6.2 Sol. Eligible Enterprise and Edu users get the same access once their workspace admin enables it. Developers can also access `gpt-6.2-astra` and `gpt-6.2-sol` through the OpenAI API, with Ultrafast available for both models at launch.

GPT‑6.2 Astra costs significantly less per task than GPT‑6 Astra, driven by better token efficiency, a 20% discount on input and output tokens, and a deeper 60% discount on cached input tokens. Standard API rates per million tokens are $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output. GPT‑6.2 Sol carries forward GPT‑6.1 Sol’s rates of $2 for input, $0.10 for cached input, and $10 for output per million tokens.

_For GPT-6.2 Astra & Sol, in order to improve cache reuse, help lower costs and latency, and preserve reasoning across turns, we recommend [keeping prompt prefixes unchanged and appending new instructions⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/preserved-reasoning) to the conversation._

Title: Introducing ChatGPT for Sales

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-for-sales

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-for-sales/

Markdown Content:
We’re introducing ChatGPT for Sales to help every sales team understand customers better, spend less time on busywork, and close more deals. It includes our new Sales plugin with dedicated skills for sellers, and more than 30 new and enhanced partner plugins in ChatGPT, so you can use information from the tools your team already relies on to prepare for calls, tailor proposals, and follow up faster.

## A starting point for every seller

The new Sales plugin from OpenAI gives you ready-to-use workflows for everyday sales work, from deciding which accounts to pursue to preparing for a call and drafting the follow-up. Sales teams work best when everyone has a shared understanding of the customer. Which accounts are worth pursuing? What does a buyer need to move forward? Which deals need attention, and why? The answers often sit across teammates, prospecting tools, customer calls, and the CRM. Bringing that information together gives teams more time to make informed decisions and follow through on customer commitments. That starts with the work you do every day.

ChatGPT for Sales launch demo.

## Connect your sales process to ChatGPT

ChatGPT for Sales brings your tools, customer context, and sales workflows into one place. It also gives your team access to partner plugins, so ChatGPT can use customer context from your existing tools to help move opportunities forward. Choose the partner plugins that fit your sales process.

![Image 1: Sales tools grouped by workflow: content and enablement, accounts and deals, prospecting, customer conversations, performance and risk, and quotes and agreements.](https://images.ctfassets.net/kftzwdyauwt9/6mmoQk1sZ7T7wZ4TZfFzA7/bc50a51cdc4d80288d4ce9fd50d1d0e6/introducing-chatgpt-for-sales-connected-tools-overview.png?w=3840&q=90&fm=webp)

*   **Create content and equip sellers**. Learn your sales process and the latest product updates with Confluence, Guru, and Seismic. Rehearse pitches and practice handling objections with ChatGPT Voice. Build tailored presentations with ChatGPT Slides, Gamma, Figma, or Canva, or create an interactive demo or ROI calculator with ChatGPT Sites.

*   **Manage accounts and advance deals**. Bring together account context from Salesforce, HubSpot, Close CRM, or monday CRM to prepare for calls, review customer commitments, and plan next steps.

*   **Find and engage buyers**. Combine account signals from Apollo, Clay, and Common Room with ChatGPT’s web research to understand what’s changing at an account and identify reasons to reach out. Use Outreach or Salesloft to plan your outreach.

*   **Turn customer conversations into action**. Use call notes from the Meetings plugin in ChatGPT, Gong, Otter.ai, or Granola to understand buyer priorities, capture agreed next steps, and draft follow-ups.

*   **Track performance and spot deal risk**. Use signals from Backstory to identify deals that need attention. Analyze connected sales data with the Data plugin in ChatGPT or Hex to explain what changed in the pipeline and where to focus next.

*   **Prepare quotes and agreements**. Bring in Docusign, Ironclad, PandaDoc, or ServiceNow CPQ to help prepare quotes and agreements when a buyer is ready to move forward.

You can also keep work moving between conversations by delegating to your [dot](https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/)—an always-on agent in ChatGPT. Your dot can use these same plugins and customer context to prepare meeting briefs, track deal updates, and proactively bring you relevant changes and proposed next steps for review.

## Use cases for every sales team

### Build pipeline in the right accounts

Use ChatGPT to build a prioritized account list from your CRM information and prospect research from tools like ZoomInfo and Clay. Ask why each account fits, identify missing information, and refine the list around your team’s priorities. Then turn that research into outreach with a specific reason to engage—all in the same conversation.

### Make a stronger case to each buyer

Before a meeting, ask for a briefing that brings together account history, previous calls, and the buyer’s priorities. Explore what still needs an answer, then turn that preparation into a customer-specific pitch with Gamma or Canva. Refine the story in the conversation before your meeting.

### Keep deals moving with clear next steps

After a call, have ChatGPT draft the follow-up, capture agreed next steps, and prepare updates to the customer record. Refine the message in the conversation and review the proposed changes. With connected tools like Attio, you can save the next step to your CRM from ChatGPT.

### See where your pipeline is at risk

Ask ChatGPT to help you understand what is holding up a deal, using CRM history and customer conversations. With Rox, you can also ask a dot to check the deal each morning, flag changes that need attention, and prepare a meeting brief or follow-up sequence for your review.

**See a few examples from across the sales ecosystem showing how these tools work in ChatGPT:**

HubSpot partner demo for ChatGPT for Sales.

**Turn context into followups**

## How sales teams are winning with ChatGPT

From account research to deal follow-through, hear how sales teams are putting ChatGPT for Sales to work.

1 of 5

## Get started

[Install the Sales plugin⁠(opens in a new window)](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/sales?openaicom-did=a0d90cbe-8aaa-40c2-bc9c-ab1c09373418&openaicom_referred=true) to get started, and [learn more about ChatGPT for Sales](https://openai.com/business/solutions/sales/) and the partner plugins. Availability of partner plugins and features varies by plan, region, and workspace settings.

ChatGPT Business and Enterprise admins can enable ChatGPT for Sales for your team by opening the[Admin Console⁠(opens in a new window)](https://admin.openai.com/), selecting your workspace, and selecting Plugins. Make the Sales plugin and relevant partner plugins available for members to install, or [install them⁠(opens in a new window)](https://help.openai.com/articles/11509118-admin-controls-security-and-compliance-for-plugins-and-apps) by default for your team. Review access to the required apps and the actions they can use. Workspace members can complete any required account connections when prompted.

We’re continuing to build ChatGPT for Sales and the partner plugin ecosystem around the work sales teams do every day. Our goal is to bring more of that work into ChatGPT, with connected tools and customer context that carries from finding an opportunity to preparing for a conversation and following through.

Title: Put Gemini to work for you

URL Source: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/tasks-in-gemini-free-new-features/

Published Time: 2026-11-17T17:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Nov 17, 2026

|

Gemini can now make the calls, pay the bills, and finish your tasks.

* * *

* * *

![Image 1: A user interface displaying the prompt "What can I get done for you?" above an input box containing placeholder text "Describe a task".](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/images/Hero_2784_x_1566.width-200.format-webp.webp)

[Audio 3](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/media/tts_audio_86987_umbriel_2026_11_18_04_46_29.mp3)

Listen to article

[[duration]] minutes

This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental

The best assistant knows you and helps you get things done. Today, you can now hand off even more tasks to Gemini and move on with your day. We’ve built it for anyone who has tasks piling up during all the classes, meetings, and school drop-offs that fill the day. Our goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.

Starting now, this update is rolling out free of charge for hundreds of millions of people across the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, using our new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. We’re also rolling out a set of advanced features, starting in the U.S.

## How it’s changing my daily routine

If your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards are already in the Google ecosystem, Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because this sensitive data already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.

Here’s how I’m using it.

Recently, our minivan’s check-engine light came on. Ugh. I pulled out Gemini and told it, "Our minivan is overdue for a service appointment. Please call the two nearest dealerships and figure out how to get an appointment early Friday morning over the next month or so."

Because Gemini already knows we drive a 2019 Honda Odyssey and where we live through [Personal Intelligence](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/personal-intelligence/), it found the nearest shops on Google Maps and called both at once [1](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/tasks-in-gemini-free-new-features/#footnote-1) . Thankfully, I didn’t have to suffer through any hold music. Gemini did the job, found a time in my Google Calendar when I was free, and added the Friday early morning appointment in less than five minutes. Done. (On the dealership's end, Gemini disclosed right away that it's an AI. Businesses can [opt out](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7690269) whenever they want, and Gemini won’t give out my payment or private account info unless I say so.)

In the background, Gemini called both dealerships at once, sat through the hold music for me, booked an appointment at the shop that accepts appointments vs. walk-ins only, and put Friday's appointment on my calendar without me having to check it.

Last month it saved us real money after we got hit with a surprise $389 electric bill. I gave Gemini permission to access our utility portal with the new Google Password Manager integration and asked for it to analyze our past billing statements in my email. Gemini worked for a few minutes, and then nailed it. The primary culprit was our heat pump, which it turns out was kicking on around 4 p.m., right in the middle of peak pricing. My wife and I never would have caught that digging through the PDFs and emails ourselves.

I use it for smaller stuff, too. For our upcoming holiday trip back to Oklahoma, I recently asked Gemini to give me the best options for a USB-C charger. Gemini quickly compared chargers thanks to Google’s Shopping Graph, asked me follow-up questions about the wattage and color, and then helped me check out using the new Google Pay integration. The best part: it also found a discount code so I saved an extra $10. Done.

Gemini now uses the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) to make purchases like this. We’re working with American Express (coming soon), Mastercard, and Visa to keep your purchases secure with digital tokens on supported cards. And when you shop with Gemini, you still earn your card's points, cashback, or purchase protections during checkout. You can also set a hard spending cap upfront, and Gemini is designed to stay within your budget. All of your receipts and tracking info land straight in Google Wallet, which is expanding to iOS [starting today](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/platforms/google-pay/wallet-available-ios-united-states/). Up next, we’ll integrate the [Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP)](https://developers.google.com/merchant/ucp) into Gemini so everyone can expect an even faster and more reliable shopping experience from discovery to checkout.

Gemini lets you set the spending limit and still earn every airline mile, cashback point, and perk on your card.

Gemini helps with weeknight dinners, too. I recently stared down a nearly empty fridge rushing out the door in the morning, and I texted Gemini with the new RCS integration [2](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/tasks-in-gemini-free-new-features/#footnote-2) : “Add lasagna, strawberries, cucumbers, and vanilla ice cream to our Instacart order.” On the walk out, I saw an empty Cheerios box in the pantry, so I snapped a photo and sent a quick follow-up: “Add this too.” Gemini added it, and then handed me off to Instacart to complete the order. Groceries were on the doorstep when we got home. Done. Today, Gemini connects with more than 60 popular apps and, as a developer, you can apply to join our [Connected Apps Platform](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/connected-apps-one-place/).

My wife and I also use Gemini to sort out medical bills, keep track of insurance renewals, and stay on top of our kids' schedules. Earlier this week, I forwarded a batch of school emails from Gmail to gemini@google.com. In less than a minute, every date was on my calendar with my wife invited. Better yet, it noticed a conflict during basketball practice and asked if I wanted to text one of the other parents to trade carpool duty.

## How we protect your data

As Gemini becomes more capable, we continually advance our security defenses. When you assign Gemini a task, it uses [Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/agent-compute-engine-deep-dive) to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users. Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams. This sandbox is just one of multiple layers of defense, including prompt-injection filters that scan search results, webpages, and more alongside Google Safe Browsing to limit which links Gemini can open.

As Gemini works on a task, you can jump in to give it more instructions at any point, and it’s also designed to pause and check with you before critical steps. For example, Gemini is designed to ask for your confirmation or pre-approval before clicking "Buy," and will ask clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous. For routine stuff you already trust, like adding those Cheerios to your grocery cart, you can set that to “Always allow” so it doesn’t pester you.

And finally, we give you access to settings and tools that help you safeguard your data and protect your privacy. You can adjust task settings, disconnect Google and third-party apps, or delete chat history anytime. For a closer look at how we’ve implemented a multi-layer defense-in-depth security strategy, read our [technical paper](https://blog.google/security/how-geminis-defense-in-depth-approach-works/).

And please participate in our bug bounty program through Google’s [AI Vulnerability Reward Program (AI VRP)](https://bughunters.google.com/about/rules/google-friends/ai-vulnerability-reward-program-rules) to advance the security of agentic systems.

## How you can help us improve

While we’ve tested tasks extensively to minimize mistakes, we haven't eliminated all of them. You may encounter situations where a task fails to complete or misses the mark. When you see this, please provide feedback by giving the response a “thumbs down.”

For example, the way personal assistants navigate the web is still evolving as sites are still adapting to these new use cases. On some sites, Gemini can make it most of the way through and then hand the screen back to you to click the final button. We’re partnering directly with major websites and security providers to help the web evolve so it works well for site owners and personal assistants. For decades, bots were blocked by default because most were malicious. Personal assistants require a more nuanced approach, and we believe open, verifiable standards will benefit everyone.

## How to try it

Ready to hand off your next task? Open Gemini, flip the home-screen toggle from Chat to Task, and tell Gemini what you need done. Starting in the U.S., you can also forward emails to [gemini@google.com](mailto:gemini@google.com) or text Gemini by following these instructions:

1.   Open Gemini on Android or iOS and tap **Settings**
2.   Tap **Channels**
3.   Tap **Set up** under **Text with Gemini**
4.   Verify your phone number

![Image 2: Texting and email setup](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/images/resized_Gemini_Tasks_-_Text__Ema.width-1200.format-webp.webp)

We can’t wait to see what Gemini crosses off your list first.

## Get the latest news from Google in your inbox

Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more.

Your information will be used in accordance with [Google's privacy policy.](https://policies.google.com/privacy) You may opt out at any time.
